textRun.content: How 5 moderated think-aloud sessions uncovered the hidden trust barriers behind an AI product's user churn — and lifted retention 12%
A trust problem disguised as a feature problem

A promising AI job-search plugin was bleeding users. Despite steady acquisition spend and a strong value prop, 70% of new users left within a week — and the team had never run UX research, building on assumptions.
As the team's first UX research consultant, uncover the root causes of abandonment — in 2 weeks, with zero recruitment budget.
Designed & solo-moderated 5 think-aloud sessions with a deliberately diverse sample (
Canada; fresh-grad to 10+ yrs; 5 industries) across 4 core tasks: visit → download → register → apply.
Core finding: users lacked trust & control, not features
Team shipped fixes → 12% relative retention lift
Roadmap pivoted to a trust-first foundation
An AI browser plugin by OOCC, a nonprofit serving job seekers, that automates job applications
“Apply to multiple jobs in 1 click. 10x your efficiency.”
Steady acquisition spend + compelling value prop
70% of new users gone within 1 week
Almost no user feedback to guide iteration
How can we improve retention if we don't know why users are leaving?
“How do we improve new-user retention and get product feedback to guide our feature roadmap?”
“What specific usability barriers cause users to abandon at each stage — and which should we fix first?”
Translating a business question into a testable research question is where UXR adds its real value
— it turns vague pain into something you can actually answer.
Competitive analysis — borrow feature ideas from rivals
Survey — ask potential users about job-search needs
Fix our own product experience before chasing new users or competitors.
Surveys need large samples; competitive analysis is slow. With zero budget, small-sample depth wins.
Fast iteration beats comprehensive-but-slow research. 5 users, 2 weeks, clear insights.
Reliable sampling on a zero-recruitment budget
No budget = no paid panels or recruiting platforms. My fix: cold outreach + targeted social-media posts.
“Flexible” never meant “random.” I tightly controlled screening so 5 participants formed a genuinely diverse sample — proof that lean recruiting doesn't mean loose sampling.
Diversity let me catch two problem types even at n=5:
(“this tool feels like it's only for new grads”).
Moderation lets me probe, clarify, catch subconscious actions
Depth over breadth. 5 sessions, 6 hours, insights impossible to get from larger but shallower studies.
vs. letting AI run analysis end-to-end
ChatGPT drafts script · I reviewed & added probes
Otter transcribes · I caught nonverbal cues
Dovetail codes · I reviewed every transcript
Fast and rigorous. AI didn't miss the details that matter — because I stayed the gatekeeper.
AI is an accelerator, not a replacement.
A researcher who doesn't review the foundational work is a researcher who misses the signal.
MY PROCESS — SOLO, END TO END
Otter captured audio; I logged body language, hesitation, frustration
Manually read every transcript ; rejected AI summaries that missed nuance
Dovetail helped code — but I drove prioritization
Live moderated session — plugin install & submission flow
users weren't struggling with UI complexity — they were afraid.
Privacy fears. Loss-of-control fears. That reframed my probes for Sessions 4–5.
Where AI accelerated — and where I stayed gatekeeper
AI accelerates; the researcher decides and validates.
Mapped domain background & surfaced preliminary hypotheses
Chose which focus areas & probes to actually pursue
Customized for business context; tuned question depth
Real-time transcription so I could stay present
Moderated live; logged hesitation & nonverbal cues
Reviewed every transcript; rejected nuance-blind takes
Pre-classified phrases by need / issue / emotion
Re-labeled by hand; drove final prioritization
Pressure-tested, sequenced, and owned the calls

Users landed on the homepage, browsed for ~5 seconds, then asked: “What is this product?” Multiple buttons all looked like download entries. They couldn't tell what it did or who built it — zero trust from second one.
“Who made this tool? Is it backed by a credible company?”
“Does it filter jobs, apply automatically, or coach me?”
Add a 5-second-clear tagline stating exactly what it does
Show a progress flow: Upload resume → AI matches → Review & apply
Display partner logos + a transparent About Us to build credibility
Four look-alike buttons — users couldn't tell which was the real CTA
Sensitive identity data requested with no consent context
The plugin connected to LinkedIn and auto-filled personal data — visa status, address, phone — without explicit consent. Users felt invaded. The same worry surfaced again and again.
“Will recruiters notice it's AI-applied? That could expose me at work.”
Privacy is the highest-stakes trust moment for an AI job product. Mishandle it and users abandon outright.
Consent-first dialog before any data transfer
Mandatory Terms & Privacy step at registration
Plain-language note: what's collected, why, how it's protected
Users want AI to save time
Users loved automation (“I can walk away and grab a coffee”) but panicked when they couldn't see or edit what the AI was doing. The fear ran deeper than wrong applications.
“If it applies for me, my boss will get pissed off.”
Users want speed AND the final say. They want to stay the gatekeeper.
Manual / semi-auto / auto modes so users pick their comfort level
“Resume preview & confirm” step before final submission
Clear start / pause controls users trust will actually stop it
The hardest evidence: the team shipped my recommendations — and described them back using my exact framing.
“Before the research, we built on gut feeling. Miranda's findings showed us where users actually got stuck — especially trust and control. That directly changed our iteration direction.”
What makes this research stand out
Designed, recruited, moderated all 5 sessions, analyzed every transcript, and presented — in 2 weeks.
Cold outreach + posts, but a deliberate mix (
Used AI for speed but stayed the gatekeeper. Reviewed every transcript; rejected summaries missing nuance.
Not just problems — also strengths to keep: the koi visuals users loved, auto-fill beating Workday, the genuine “wow.”
No budget, no team, 2-week deadline forced smarter work. The constraints drove rigor, not around it.
“In an age of AI, what part of UX research should a human never delegate?”
Foundational, insight-related work — even the tedious, repetitive parts — should stay human-led.
To correct AI and give precise instructions, a UXR must know the details more deeply than the AI does.
Every tool I tested nailed high-level summaries but consistently missed the details.
AI can't feel the degree of a user's frustration — the real anxiety behind “my boss will get pissed off.”
“AI can accelerate analysis, but it can't feel what the user feels.”
I love having AI as my assistant — but I value my intuition and empathy even more.
Invite stakeholders to observe 2–3 sessions live — seeing beats reading a report
Pilot the script first — I caught awkward wording only after Session 2
